title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what a modal really does, and which pronoun comes back

questions.prompt: A classmate says: "I will be glad to help you with the revision any time you ask." Your exercise asks you to tick what the sentence expresses, and the table has six columns: regret, advice, reproach, deduction, unnecessary action, offering help. Which column takes this sentence?

options.text: advice
offering help
deduction
unnecessary action

questions.explanation: will here carries a decision taken at the moment of speaking, and what is decided is to make oneself available — an offer, which is the column the table keeps for it. Calling it advice would mean the speaker is telling somebody else what to do, and he is not: he is saying what he himself will do. Deduction would need evidence and a conclusion drawn from it, which is the work of must, and there is nothing here to conclude from. And unnecessary action is what needn't declares, the opposite of an offer. If you were told this sentence is simply a future, notice that the table has no such column — the tense is real, but it is not what the sentence does.

questions.prompt: Two sentences describe the same class. (1) "They looked at themselves." (2) "They looked at each other." What does the first one say that the second does not?

options.text: That each pupil looked at his own reflection.
That the pupils exchanged glances.
That somebody outside the class looked at them.
That only one pupil was looking.

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun turns the action back on the person who performs it, so each pupil in the first sentence is looking at himself, in a mirror or a window. The second sentence is the one that describes glances travelling between people, and that is precisely what each other means: the action goes from one to another rather than back to its own doer. Nobody outside the class is involved in either sentence, since both subjects are they and both objects point inside the group. And themselves is plural, so it cannot narrow the scene down to a single pupil; the number is fixed by the subject, which is plural in both.

questions.prompt: A caretaker leaves two notes on the same door. Note one: "You mustn't use this exit after six." Note two: "You needn't lock this door; it locks itself." Which statement about the two notes is true?

options.text: Both notes forbid an action.
The first forbids, the second says the action serves no purpose.
Both notes say the action is unnecessary.
The first says the action is unnecessary, the second forbids it.

questions.explanation: mustn't closes the exit: it names something that is not allowed, and breaking it would be breaking a rule. needn't leaves the door entirely open and merely tells you the effort is wasted, since the lock does the work by itself — the second half of the note gives the reason. Reading both as prohibitions makes the caretaker forbid locking a door, which no caretaker would; reading both as unnecessary makes the six o'clock rule optional, which empties it of meaning. And swapping them round is the commonest error of the whole chapter, because must and need feel like neighbours while their negatives point in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Your book asks you to read only the introduction and the opening line of each paragraph of the uniform text, and to say whether it is descriptive, argumentative or expository. Each opening line states a position: "Well I think they're a good idea, because…", "It distinguishes you from other schools…", "I think that by putting us all in the same uniform, they suppress our identities…". What kind of text is it, and what makes the openings enough to tell?

options.text: Expository, because it explains how a school system works.
Descriptive, because it tells you what the school uniforms look like.
Argumentative, because every opening states a position.
Descriptive, because it reports what several people said.
Expository, because it presents both sides without choosing.

questions.explanation: An argumentative text defends positions, and every opening here does exactly that: one announces a good idea and gives a because, another claims a benefit, a third makes an accusation. That is why the openings alone settle the question — the position always arrives first, and the support follows. An expository text would explain how something works without taking sides, and no speaker in this text is neutral. A descriptive text would tell you what the uniforms look like, which the text never does; and reporting what people said is not description either, since what is reported is opinion. Finally, the text does contain both sides, but it does not present them without choosing: each individual speaker chooses, and it is the collection that is balanced.

questions.prompt: A pupil rewrites her homework three times. Which sentence uses its modal correctly for the meaning given in brackets?

options.text: You needn't cheat in an examination. (it is forbidden)
I shouldn't have revised the passive, and I am very glad that I did. (regret)
He must have forgotten his umbrella; look how wet he is. (past deduction)
You had better to arrive early. (urgent advice)

questions.explanation: must plus have plus a past participle draws a conclusion about something already over, and the wet coat is the evidence the conclusion rests on, so the sentence and its label agree. The first sentence uses needn't for a prohibition, and needn't never forbids — cheating calls for mustn't. The second contradicts itself: shouldn't have blames somebody for what was done, so it cannot sit beside I am glad I did, and regret over one's own omission would be I should have revised. And the last one keeps to after had better, which takes the base verb alone — the label is right, the form is not.

questions.prompt: In lesson 19, Barbara says she wishes she had started her revision before last week, that she was up very late the night before, and that she then could not sleep because she was so worried. Which advice answers her, and why is it not the one about keeping calm?

options.text: Don't revise at the last minute; sleep well the night before.
Keep calm; if you've done your revision, there's no need to panic.
Plan your time in the exam; look through the whole paper first.
Use your revision plan and spend most of your time on the things you are not sure of.

questions.explanation: Barbara names two things — she began far too late, and she lost her night's sleep because of it — and one piece of advice names both, telling her not to revise heavily at the last minute and to sleep before the exam. Keeping calm is addressed to a pupil who did revise properly and whose mind has gone blank all the same, which is Andy; Barbara's trouble is not panic in the room but a plan that collapsed before she reached it. Planning your time inside the exam answers Steve, who left a whole section unread. And using a revision plan to target what you do not know answers Jane, who spent her time on what she already knew.
